questions.stem: A binomial X has mean 4 and variance 3.2. What is n?
questions.incorrectFeedback: Divide: q = npq/np = 3.2/4 = 0.8. Then p = 0.2 and n = np/p = 4/0.2 = 20.

options: tosses needed to get the first head
aces among 5 cards dealt without replacing
heads in 10 tosses of one coin
rainy days in a year of weather
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — fixed n = 10, independent tosses, same p, counting heads: BINS.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Only heads in 10 tosses passes BINS. Tosses-until-a-head has no fixed n; cards without replacement aren't independent; rainy days don't share one p and aren't independent.

questions.stem: Someone claims a binomial with mean 3 and variance 4. This is…
options: fine, whenever n is large enough
impossible, since variance exceeds the mean
questions.correctFeedback: Right — q = 4/3 would exceed 1. A binomial's variance npq is always below its mean np.
questions.incorrectFeedback: q = variance/mean = 4/3 > 1, which no probability can be. A binomial always has variance below its mean.

questions.stem: From Lesson 7: Var(X) = 3. What is Var(3 − X)?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the shift 3 drops out and (−1)² = 1, so the variance stays 3.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Var(a + bX) = b²Var(X). Here b = −1, so (−1)² × 3 = 3. A variance is never negative.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled 4 times. P(at least one six) is…
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — the complement of 'at least one six' is 'no sixes', with chance (5/6)⁴.
questions.incorrectFeedback: Use the complement: P(no six in 4) = (5/6)⁴, so P(at least one) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518. Adding 1/6 four times double-counts.
